name: Question 6
problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=\frac{4{x}^{2}}{y}\,,\,y>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$*
worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,⟹\,y={(z+{x}^{2})}^{1/2}\,.
$$

]
Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x).
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x)+(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2} & =\frac{4{x}^{2}}{(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2}} \\ x(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x)+2(z+{x}^{2}) & =8{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x+\frac{2}{x}(z+{x}^{2}) & =8x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/x\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot 4x \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & ={x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

Question 6
?

Find the general solution to the following equation. xdydx+y=4x2y,y>0

Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution z=y2−x2.

a
y=x2+Cx
b
y=2x2+Cx2
c
y=2x+Cx2
d
y=Cx2+2x2
e
y=x+Cx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=y2−x2⟹y=(z+x2)1/2. ] Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get

dzdx=2ydydx−2x⟹dydx=12(z+x2)1/2(dzdx+2x).

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of z as follows:

x2(z+x2)1/2(dzdx+2x)+(z+x2)1/2=4x2(z+x2)1/2x(dzdx+2x)+2(z+x2)=8x2

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form: dzdx+2x+2x(z+x2)=8xdzdx+2xz=4x

The above equation is in the standard form dzdx+P(x)y=Q(x)

with

P(x)=2x,Q(x)=4x.

We then compute an integrating factor:

I(x)=e∫P(x)dx=e∫2/xdx=e2ln⁡x=eln⁡x2=x2

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by I(x)=x2 yields

x2⋅(dzdx+2xz)=x2⋅4xx2⋅dzdx+2xz=4x3ddx(x2z)=4x3

Now, we integrate with respect to x: ∫ddx(x2z)dx=∫4x3dxx2z=x4+Cz=x2+Cx2

Finally, we determine y(x) by writing z=y2−x2. This results in

y2−x2=x2+Cx2y2=2x2+Cx2y=2x2+Cx2, where we used that y>0.
